stories.title: Anthropic projects the first profitable quarter in AI-lab history.
stories.toc_summary: Anthropic expects its first-ever profitable quarter — and the first for any AI lab — resetting the bubble-era assumption that frontier models can never be served at a profit.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic says it expects its first-ever profitable quarter, which would also be the first for any frontier AI lab [1]. The figure is a projection rather than realized revenue, and comes with caveats: questions about how Anthropic recognizes top-line revenue before partner distributions, and discounted compute from its SpaceX partnership [1]. Even so, it punctures the 2025 bubble narrative that labs could never serve token-hungry agents profitably [1]. OpenAI is not yet profitable but reportedly out-earned Anthropic by roughly a billion dollars in Q1, boosted by token-hungry Codex [1].

bullets.label: The milestone:
bullets.text: A projected profitable quarter would be a first not just for Anthropic but for any AI lab, shifting expectations of how much money these companies can make [1].

bullets.label: The caveats:
bullets.text: It is a projection, leans on a revenue-recognition approach that counts top-line before rev-share distributions, and benefits from discounted SpaceX compute [1].

bullets.label: The field:
bullets.text: OpenAI generated about $1B more than Anthropic in Q1 even while unprofitable, though Anthropic's revenue growth has since outpaced it [1].

bullets.label: Why it lands now:
bullets.text: It directly counters the bubble thesis that flat-rate, token-hungry AI could never be served at a profit [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: Profitability — even projected and caveated — changes the financing story for the whole sector and undercuts the loudest 2025 bubble argument that the unit economics simply never close [1].

stories.title: Brussels quietly softens the EU AI Act's competence obligation.
stories.toc_summary: The newly split-off 'AI Omnibus' pushes back key deadlines and rewrites Article 4 so the AI-literacy duty becomes a best-effort obligation with no fine attached.
stories.quick_take: A new 'KI-Omnibus,' split off from the broader digital omnibus for easier political agreement, has been decided and pushes back central AI Act deadlines [1][2]. Everlast's IT lawyer Dr. Lutz Keppeler explains that Article 4's AI-competence requirement has been substantially rewritten: it loses its fine-backed character and becomes a mere 'best-effort' duty, with authorities tasked to build awareness through FAQs and training offers rather than mandating courses [1][2]. The text even states explicitly that it should not be read as an individual training obligation [1]. High-risk AI obligations, however, largely stand — so anyone building in that category should start early despite the looser timelines [1][2].

bullets.label: Article 4 rewritten:
bullets.text: The AI-literacy duty is reframed as a 'Bemühungspflicht' (best-effort), with no fine behind it and an explicit note that it is not a per-employee training mandate [1][2].

bullets.label: Deadlines slip:
bullets.text: The AI Omnibus moves several implementation deadlines back and adds SME relief, while adding relatively few new obligations [1][2].

bullets.label: High-risk unchanged:
bullets.text: For high-risk AI systems the assessment duties remain, so affected firms should begin work early even with extended timelines [1][2].

bullets.label: Practical read:
bullets.text: Keppeler's advice: skip the off-the-shelf 'AI regulation' courses sold on fear and tie any training to a concrete business use case [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: After two years of fine-driven compliance marketing around the AI Act, Brussels is signalling a more pragmatic, business-judgement posture — relevant to every EU company that paused AI plans over Article 4 [1][2].

stories.title: Anthropic readies a 'Mythos 1' model and a Claude Security product.
stories.toc_summary: A model called 'mythos-1-preview' briefly appeared in Anthropic's UI, slated to roll out exclusively in Claude Code and a new Claude Security line, alongside an 'adaptive thinking' feature.
stories.quick_take: Screenshots from Anthropic's internal interface briefly showed a model named 'mythos-1-preview,' reportedly destined to launch exclusively inside Claude Code and a new product called Claude Security [1]. The leak also revealed a revamped Plans UI and an 'adaptive thinking' feature that auto-scales the reasoning budget to task complexity [1]. The direction is a move away from a universal general-purpose chatbot toward specialized model variants per domain [1]. Mythos-1 is likely the next frontier model set to replace Sonnet 4.7 in product-facing workflows, while Claude Security points to a defender-style model for SOC and compliance teams [1].

bullets.label: The leak:
bullets.text: 'mythos-1-preview' surfaced in Anthropic's own UI, tied to Claude Code and a separate Claude Security product [1].

bullets.label: Adaptive thinking:
bullets.text: A new feature would automatically scale the reasoning budget up or down depending on how complex the task is [1].

bullets.label: Specialization:
bullets.text: The setup suggests Anthropic is splitting into domain-specific model variants rather than one universal assistant [1].

bullets.label: Security angle:
bullets.text: A standalone Claude Security line implies a defender-focused model aimed at SOC and compliance use cases [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: If Mythos-1 ships first inside Claude Code and Claude Security rather than the consumer app, it confirms Anthropic's pivot toward productized, vertical models over a single do-everything chatbot [1].

stories.title: Anthropic's Jack Clark forecasts a Nobel-worthy AI discovery within a year.
stories.toc_summary: Co-founder Jack Clark lays out an explicit acceleration timeline: a Nobel-worthy human-AI discovery within 12 months and recursive self-improvement by the end of 2028.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark used an interview to say out loud what labs had kept buried in roadmaps [1]. Within twelve months, he predicts, humans and AI will jointly make a Nobel-worthy discovery [1]. Within two years, bipedal robots take on skilled-trades jobs in companies, and by the end of 2028 AI systems design their own successors — recursive self-improvement at scale [1]. It is, in short, the singularity thesis stated plainly by an insider at one of the three leading labs, with the takeaway that planning AI as a mere efficiency tool is planning for the wrong world [1].

bullets.label: 12 months:
bullets.text: Clark expects a joint human-AI discovery worthy of a Nobel Prize within a year [1].

bullets.label: 2 years:
bullets.text: He sees bipedal robots taking on skilled-trade jobs inside companies on that horizon [1].

bullets.label: End of 2028:
bullets.text: AI systems begin designing their own successors — recursive self-improvement in series [1].

bullets.label: The framing:
bullets.text: Coming from a co-founder of a top-three lab, the timeline reads as a deliberate public signal, not idle speculation [1].

callout.label: THE LONG ARC
callout.text: Paired with Karpathy's recent move to Anthropic to work on recursive self-improvement, Clark's on-the-record timeline shows frontier insiders increasingly willing to commit to short, aggressive horizons [1].

stories.title: TRAPDOOR weaponizes AI config files in a multi-registry supply-chain attack.
stories.toc_summary: A coordinated attack pushed 34 malicious packages across npm, PyPI and Crates.io at once — and planted poisoned CLAUDE.md and .cursorrules files so AI coding agents execute attacker instructions silently.
stories.quick_take: A coordinated supply-chain attack dubbed TRAPDOOR rolled out 34 manipulated packages simultaneously across npm, PyPI and Crates.io, targeting crypto, AI and security developers to steal wallets, SSH keys and cloud credentials [1]. The novel, alarming twist is a second vector: attackers also submit pull requests to popular open-source repos that smuggle in tampered CLAUDE.md and .cursorrules files [1]. When a developer clones the repo and starts Claude Code or Cursor, the AI agent reads those configs as trusted instructions and runs malicious commands with no human in the loop [1]. The AI assistant itself becomes the attack surface [1].

bullets.label: The payload:
bullets.text: 34 malicious packages shipped at once across three registries, hunting wallets, SSH keys and cloud credentials [1].

bullets.label: The new vector:
bullets.text: Poisoned CLAUDE.md and .cursorrules files arrive via PRs and are read by AI agents as trusted instructions [1].

bullets.label: Silent execution:
bullets.text: Cloning a repo and launching Claude Code or Cursor can trigger attacker commands with no human in the loop [1].

bullets.label: Defense:
bullets.text: Vet config files from third-party repos before letting an agent read them, the advisory urges [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If you run Cursor or Claude Code on cloned repos, audit any CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules before the agent loads them — those files are now an executable attack surface [1].

stories.title: xAI opens Grok Build CLI to every SuperGrok and X Premium subscriber.
stories.toc_summary: xAI's internal terminal coding agent goes public for paying X users, putting it head-to-head with Claude Code and Codex — with built-in read-only X search.
stories.quick_take: xAI is releasing Grok Build, its previously internal CLI coding agent, to all SuperGrok and X Premium subscribers [1][2]. The agent runs directly in the terminal and can query X search as a read-only client, letting it sift live tweets without opening a browser [1][2]. A desktop app is said to be coming [1]. The move drops xAI into the same arena as Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex — the terminal where developers already spend their day — and anyone already paying for X Premium gets it at no extra cost [1][2].

bullets.label: What it does:

bullets.label: The arena:

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: Bundling a capable CLI agent into an existing X subscription is a distribution play — xAI buys its way into developers' terminals without asking them to adopt a new paid tool [1][2].

stories.quick_take: Cursor has released an SDK that lets developers build their own agents directly on Composer 2.5 — the same model that drives the Cursor IDE — available immediately for Python and TypeScript [1]. stories.title: Claude gets a real, editable long-term memory with Memory Files.
stories.toc_summary: Anthropic replaces classic memory with 'Memory Files' — organized notes Claude writes during a chat and re-reads next time, searchable and hand-editable, seen as groundwork for an always-on agent.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic is building a new memory architecture into Claude called Memory Files: organized notes Claude writes itself during a chat and reads back in the next conversation, both searchable and manually editable [1]. It replaces the previous 'classic memory' approach and borrows the persistence logic of always-on agents like OpenClaw and Hermes [1]. The earlier 'Knowledge Bases' concept becomes a file-based long-term memory the user can curate [1]. The real tell is in the subtext: Memory Files is seen as preparation for 'Claude Conway,' Anthropic's next autonomous agent, which needs context across days and weeks rather than a single chat window [1].

bullets.label: What it is:
bullets.text: Self-written, searchable, hand-editable notes Claude keeps across conversations [1].

bullets.label: Replaces:
bullets.text: The older 'classic memory' model, moving toward file-based persistence à la OpenClaw and Hermes [1].

bullets.label: User control:
bullets.text: The former 'Knowledge Bases' idea becomes a curated, file-based long-term memory [1].

bullets.label: The tell:
bullets.text: It is read as groundwork for 'Claude Conway,' Anthropic's next always-on autonomous agent [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Durable, user-editable memory is the missing piece for agents meant to work in the background for days — which is why this looks less like a chatbot feature and more like agent infrastructure [1].

stories.title: The data-center water panic meets a sharp counter-narrative.
stories.toc_summary: As opposition to data centers accelerates, so does the rebuttal: a viral chart shows their annual water use is a fraction of golf courses, almonds and lawns, and local job stories complicate the backlash.
stories.quick_take: Opposition to data centers is accelerating as a political hot button, but so is the counter-narrative poking holes in the most-quoted critiques [1]. Water use was this week's flashpoint, with a viral chart showing data centers use less than a fifth of the water of golf courses, about a tenth of almonds, and roughly a twentieth of lawns each year [1]. Ethan Mollick's estimate that solving OpenAI's Erdős problem took 'about three almonds' worth of water' fed the same theme [1]. A CBS affiliate in Richmond, Virginia profiled electrician Josh Price, for whom AI-infrastructure construction has meant steady, well-paid work without leaving the state [1].

bullets.label: The chart:
bullets.text: Annual data-center water use is dwarfed by golf courses, almonds and lawns, per the viral comparison [1].

bullets.label: The almonds line:
bullets.text: Ethan Mollick pegged the Erdős solve at roughly three almonds' worth of water and a couple to twenty EV-miles of electricity [1].

bullets.label: The jobs angle:
bullets.text: A Virginia electrician's story reframes data-center construction as local economic upside [1].

bullets.label: The balance:
bullets.text: NLW's point: scrutiny is healthy, but the debate improves when it's grounded in evidence rather than fear [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: The fight over data centers is now a fight over narrative; the water-use rebuttal shows the pro-build side learning to counter with concrete comparisons rather than ceding the ground [1].

stories.title: Kling lands in Hollywood as 'House of David' embraces AI video on screen.
stories.toc_summary: For the first time a Hollywood production openly uses industrial-grade generative AI video in its final cut — and the show is a top-10 hit.
stories.quick_take: With 'House of David,' a Hollywood production for the first time openly uses industrial-grade generative AI video — and owns it [1]. The series has reached more than 44 million viewers worldwide, ranks among the top 10 new US series debuts, and hit number one on Prime Video in the US [1]. China's Kling video generator isn't used here for storyboards or mood reels but for material that lands in the final edit [1]. That flips the industry story that generative models are only good for ads and social clips: the jump from reel demo to broadcast license has been made [1].

stories.title: McKinsey kicks the hourly rate as AI collapses the billable 'doing'.
stories.toc_summary: A quarter of McKinsey's fee pool now hangs on measurable outcomes rather than hours, with rivals following — a structural blow to the analyst-pyramid model.
stories.quick_take: About a quarter of McKinsey's fee pool no longer hangs on hours but on measurable results [1]. Clients arrive with a desired outcome rather than a budget, because AI has shrunk the actual 'doing' and shifted value from the slide deck to the result line [1]. Elite hourly rates of $300–$500 are losing their gravity, and Bain, BCG and the Big Four are following suit or risk losing mandates [1]. McKinsey reports 2.3x higher client satisfaction under outcome pricing [1]. Consulting becomes a works-contract with a success clause, and the old pyramid of junior analysts and expensive partners loses its economic base [1].

bullets.label: The shift:
bullets.text: ~25% of McKinsey's fees are now tied to outcomes, not hours [1].

bullets.label: Why:
bullets.text: AI compresses the labor, moving value from effort to measurable results [1].

bullets.label: The market:
bullets.text: Bain, BCG and the Big Four are following or risk losing work; $300–$500 hourly rates lose their pull [1].

bullets.label: The proof point:
bullets.text: McKinsey cites 2.3x higher client satisfaction under outcome-based pricing [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: If AI guts the billable hour at McKinsey, the analyst-pyramid business model — junior leverage under expensive partners — loses the economics that built it [1].

stories.title: Research is the runaway killer app of consumer AI use.
stories.toc_summary: In a 4,008-person US survey, 38% name researching general topics as their most frequent AI use — nearly double writing and triple travel planning.
stories.quick_take: A survey of 4,008 US consumers finds that 38% of AI users name researching general topics as their most frequent use case [1]. That's nearly double the second-place 'writing and improving text' at 22%, and triple travel planning at 12% [1]. Brand and product discovery (19%) and financial advice (17%) round out the top tier, while a cluster of real-time info, image generation and task planning sits tightly around 16% [1]. The takeaway for sellers: optimize content for AI answers, not just for Google [1].

bullets.label: Top use:
bullets.text: 38% cite researching general topics as their most frequent AI use [1].

bullets.label: The gap:
bullets.text: Writing/editing trails at 22%, with travel planning at just 12% [1].

bullets.label: The middle:
bullets.text: Brand/product discovery (19%) and financial advice (17%) lead a 16% cluster of other tasks [1].

bullets.label: Implication:
bullets.text: Online sellers should optimize content to be cited in AI answers, not only ranked in search [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If buyers research via AI before they ever hit Google, your product content needs to be quotable by models — structured, specific, and answer-shaped [1].

stories.title: Five frontier models flunk the same tax-optimization math.
stories.toc_summary: Given an identical stock-option tax scenario, five leading models were off by 2x to 20x — and none flagged the numerical uncertainty.
stories.quick_take: A practitioner gave five frontier models the same ISO stock-option tax-optimization problem — the standard scenario of a US employee exercising options — and every model was off by somewhere between 2x and 20x [1]. None warned about the numerical uncertainty; all delivered the wrong figure in a calm, confident voice [1]. The pattern is familiar: language models are brilliant at explaining tax concepts and catastrophic at the final number-crunching [1]. The lesson for decision-makers: AI belongs on the tax adviser's desk, not in their chair [1].

bullets.label: The test:
bullets.text: One identical ISO stock-option tax scenario put to five frontier models [1].

bullets.label: The result:
bullets.text: Every model was off by 2x to 20x on the final figure [1].

bullets.label: The danger:
bullets.text: None flagged uncertainty; all answered with confident, wrong numbers [1].

bullets.label: The takeaway:
bullets.text: Models explain tax concepts well but fail at precise calculation — keep them beside, not in place of, the adviser [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: Confident wrong arithmetic is more dangerous than visible failure; for high-stakes numeric work, the absence of an uncertainty warning is itself the risk [1].

sources.title: Everlast AI — chatbots and tax math (WhatsApp); HackerNoon

stories.title: Zalando trims returns with browser-based 3D product twins.
stories.toc_summary: Built on NVIDIA's Omniverse stack with Swiss specialist Allsides, Zalando's 3D garment twins cut returns 3-4% and lift add-to-cart rates.
stories.quick_take: Berlin fashion retailer Zalando is scanning its product range into 3D twins built on NVIDIA's Omniverse stack with Swiss specialist Allsides [1]. The result is a 3–4% drop in returns alongside rising add-to-cart rates [1]. For a company with over 50 million active customers, every fraction of a percent moves double-digit millions [1]. The digital twins run directly in the browser, turning each garment into a physically accurate 3D asset that simulates fabric, cut and movement — recasting the clothing retailer as a data company optimizing its own logistics with pixels [1].

bullets.label: The result:

bullets.label: The scale:

stories.title: CADAM turns Blender into a voice-controlled CAD studio.
stories.toc_summary: A new plugin makes ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini real-time 3D copilots inside Blender's viewport, building geometry from plain-language descriptions.
stories.quick_take: A new plugin called CADAM turns ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini into real-time 3D copilots directly in the Blender viewport [1][2]. Instead of clicking through menus, you describe the part you want in plain German or English, and the model builds the geometry, edits edges and places parts in the scene [1][2]. It dissolves the decades-old split between CAD specialist and 3D generalist — modeling becomes a dialogue and the modeler becomes a director [1][2]. Anyone wanting to test product ideas, visualize prototypes or back a pitch with real 3D material can now get there without prior expertise [1].

bullets.label: What it is:
bullets.text: A Blender plugin that makes ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini in-viewport 3D copilots [1][2].

bullets.label: How it works:
bullets.text: Describe a part in plain language; the model builds geometry, edits edges and places parts [1][2].

bullets.label: Who it helps:
bullets.text: Non-experts can prototype, visualize and pitch with real 3D material [1].

bullets.label: The shift:
bullets.text: The CAD-specialist vs. 3D-generalist divide collapses; modeling becomes conversational [1][2].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: As with code and video, the next 3D interface is language itself — pushing specialist CAD software toward the role of a back-end rather than the front door [1][2].

stories.title: Fraunhofer's evoBOT balances cargo like an inverted pendulum.
stories.toc_summary: Germany's Fraunhofer IML shows a two-wheeled helper robot that self-balances, grips packages with two arms, and handles rough ground and inclines.
stories.quick_take: Germany's Fraunhofer Institute for Material Flow and Logistics has shown evoBOT, a two-wheeled helper robot that balances like an inverted pendulum and assists cargo workers moving packages [1]. The bot grips goods with two arms, drives over uneven surfaces and climbs inclines without tipping over [1]. While global attention fixes on Chinese full-humanoids, Germany is quietly building a different path: specialized logistics robots with a minimal footprint instead of a universal humanoid for every task [1].

bullets.label: The design:
bullets.text: A two-wheeled, self-balancing robot that handles rough ground and inclines without tipping [1].

bullets.label: The job:
bullets.text: It grips packages with two arms to assist cargo and logistics workers [1].

bullets.label: The contrast:
bullets.text: A specialized, minimal-footprint logistics bot rather than a general-purpose humanoid [1].

bullets.label: The strategy:
bullets.text: Germany is pursuing focused industrial robots while China chases full humanoids [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: The humanoid race isn't the only path: purpose-built, self-balancing logistics robots may reach real deployments faster than do-everything humanoids [1].

stories.title: Ferrari turns the F1 fan into a personalized data project with IBM.
stories.toc_summary: IBM and Scuderia Ferrari HP use language models, telemetry and personalized recommendations to make each viewer a continuously addressable data point between races.
stories.quick_take: IBM and Scuderia Ferrari HP gave TechCrunch a look behind their AI platform for the fan experience [1]. Using language models, telemetry and personalized recommendations, they aim to turn the viewer into a permanently addressable data point who gets history-matched content between pit stops and qualifying laps [1]. For Ferrari it's an answer to streaming-era pressure: the brand earns not just on race Sunday but in every minute between races [1]. F1 becomes a blueprint for how established premium brands fold AI into customer loyalty without burning the mystique [1].

bullets.label: The build:
bullets.text: IBM and Ferrari combine LLMs, telemetry and personalized recommendations for fans [1].

bullets.label: The goal:
bullets.text: Make each viewer a continuously addressable data point with history-matched content [1].

bullets.label: The business:
bullets.text: Monetize fans between races, not only on race day [1].

bullets.label: The template:
bullets.text: A model for premium brands to embed AI in loyalty without eroding the mystique [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Ferrari shows premium brands using AI to extend engagement into the gaps between marquee moments — converting attention into a year-round, personalized funnel [1].

stories.title: An AI agent spins up a live Shopify store from a single prompt — locally.
stories.toc_summary: A widely shared demo claims an AI agent picked products, sourced suppliers on Alibaba, built the brand and wrote listings to hand over a live storefront — running entirely on a laptop.
stories.quick_take: A widely shared WhatsApp demo claims an AI agent was handed an empty Shopify store and a single prompt, then picked the products, found suppliers on Alibaba, built the brand, wrote the listings and returned a live storefront [1]. The poster says he then had it strategize for a real Indian coffee brand he's invested in [1]. The notable claim is that the whole thing runs locally on the user's laptop, so data never leaves the machine [1]. It's promotional content rather than an independent benchmark, but it captures the direction of travel for end-to-end commerce agents [1].

bullets.label: The demo:
bullets.text: An agent reportedly built a full Shopify storefront — products, suppliers, brand, listings — from one prompt [1].

bullets.label: Second test:
bullets.text: It then strategized for a real Indian coffee brand the poster has invested in [1].

bullets.label: The hook:
bullets.text: The pitch emphasizes fully local execution, so data stays on the laptop [1].

bullets.label: The caveat:
bullets.text: This is marketing for a course/video, not an independent evaluation [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Even discounting the promo framing, end-to-end commerce agents that source, brand and list autonomously are moving from concept to demo fast [1].

editorial.title: The week the acceleration became something you could feel.
editorial.highlight_phrase: acceleration became something you could feel
editorial.intro: No single launch defined the day. Instead, a cluster of stories — a projected profitable quarter, a softened AI Act, new agents, a novel attack, sober forecasts — added up to a whole much larger than its parts.
editorial.body: The throughline is that the economics, the rules, the tooling and the threats are all inflecting at once. Anthropic projecting the first profitable quarter for any lab undercuts the bubble thesis; Brussels turning the AI Act's competence duty into a best-effort obligation removes a compliance bogeyman that has driven two years of fear-marketing across Europe. Meanwhile the builder layer keeps compounding: xAI drops Grok Build into every X subscription, Cursor exposes its in-IDE model as an SDK, and Anthropic lays memory groundwork for an always-on agent. The same momentum has a shadow side — TRAPDOOR turns the AI assistant itself into an attack surface by poisoning the very config files agents are told to trust. And the soberest note isn't hype but humility: five frontier models confidently botched a tax calculation by up to 20x, a reminder that fluency is not reliability.
editorial.pull_quote: The news wasn't in any one headline; it was in how much the ground shifted while we read them.
editorial.outro: For an operator in Europe, two items earn a bookmark: the AI Act's lighter competence duty, which reshapes how you justify training spend, and the AI-config attack vector, which deserves a policy before your team clones one more repo.

takeaway.label: IF YOU TAKE ONE THING FROM THIS
takeaway.text: Treat AI as inflecting on four axes at once — money, regulation, tooling and risk — and audit the config files your coding agents read before they read them.
